post_text:
I capped our HikariCP pool at ten connections per pod when we launched checkout.

Everyone asked why we were deliberately choking throughput before the first customer arrived.

The team wanted fifty connections per replica, pointing to synthetic benchmarks with higher concurrency.

I spent launch night staring at Grafana, terrified that a modest traffic spike would exhaust the tiny pool, queue threads, and prove my stubbornness wrong.

Six months later, an unindexed query slipped into production during a flash sale. While request latency climbed and application queues filled, the Postgres primary stayed healthy at forty percent CPU because total active connections remained strictly bounded across the fleet.

Downstream systems experienced degraded responses instead of a cascading database crash that would have halted operations.

We deployed the missing index in twenty minutes without ever needing to restart the database.

What I learned:

Sizing connection pools to the physical limits of the database rather than the optimism of application threads keeps failures survivable.
